blocks.html: A probability sample is one in which every unit in the population has a known, non-zero chance of selection. That known chance is what lets the formal machinery of estimation (Chapter 7) attach a margin of error (how far the result may plausibly lie from the population value by chance alone) to a sample result. Most probability methods need a sampling frame: a list, map or register from which units are drawn, such as a village register, an anganwadi child list or a Census list of villages. The six sections below run from the simplest design (simple random sampling) to the large survey designs used by Indian programmes.

blocks.alt: Four probability sampling methods applied to the same population
blocks.caption: Figure 6.1. Four probability sampling methods applied to the same population.

blocks.html: Simple Random Sampling

blocks.label: Definition
blocks.html: Simple random sampling (SRS) selects n units from N so that every possible sample of size n has the same chance of being chosen. This implies that every unit has the same chance of inclusion, n/N. The reverse is not true: other designs (systematic sampling, cluster sampling with equal-sized clusters) also give every unit the chance n/N but are not SRS, because many possible samples can never occur under them.

blocks.label: Simplified Explanation
blocks.html: SRS is the “equally likely outcomes” idea of classical probability (recall §5.1.1) applied to choosing people instead of rolling dice. No subgroup is favoured, and no combination of units is ruled out. When sampling is without replacement, the draws are not independent of each other: once a person is drawn, they cannot be drawn again, which changes the chances for everyone left. What defines SRS is the equal chance of every possible sample, not independence.

blocks.label: Illustration / Example
blocks.html: Number every child on an anganwadi register of 1,000, then use a random number generator to pick 100 distinct numbers. Every child, whatever their age or hamlet, had the chance 100/1,000 = 0.1 of inclusion, and every set of 100 children was equally likely to be the sample.

points.html: SRS needs a complete, current sampling frame of individual units. Building that frame is often the hardest part in the field.

SRS is the reference design: the formulas for standard errors in §6.5–6.7 and Chapter 7 are derived for it. Other designs are judged by how far their precision departs from SRS of the same size (the design effect, §6.2.6).
For large, scattered populations SRS is costly: randomly chosen households across a state means travelling to every corner of it. This is why cluster and multistage designs (§6.2.4–6.2.5) exist.

blocks.html: Systematic Sampling

blocks.label: Definition
blocks.html: Systematic sampling arranges the population in a list and selects every kth unit after a random start between 1 and k, where the sampling interval k = N ÷ n.

blocks.label: Simplified Explanation
blocks.html: One random number sets the start; after that you count forward by k. This is much easier in the field than drawing n random numbers, and every unit still has the chance 1/k = n/N of selection. But only k different samples are possible (one per starting point), not all the combinations SRS allows. That is harmless when the list order is unrelated to what you measure, and dangerous when the list has a cycle that lines up with k.

blocks.label: Illustration / Example
blocks.html: To sample 100 patients from a clinic register of 1,000: k = 1,000 ÷ 100 = 10. A random start between 1 and 10 gives, say, 7. The sample is patients 7, 17, 27, … 997, which is 100 patients. Only 10 distinct samples are possible, one for each start from 1 to 10.

points.html: k = N ÷ n; the start is random between 1 and k; every unit has inclusion chance 1/k.

Periodicity risk: if the list repeats in a cycle that matches k (for example, a ward register where every 10th bed is the high-dependency bed), every selected unit falls at the same point in the cycle and the estimate is biased. SRS cannot fail this way.
A list sorted by a relevant variable (village size, literacy) gives an implicit stratification that usually improves precision. NFHS-5 sorts its lists this way before selecting (§6.2.5).

blocks.html: Stratified Sampling

blocks.label: Definition
blocks.html: Stratified sampling divides the population into non-overlapping subgroups (strata) on a relevant characteristic, then draws a separate random sample within every stratum.

blocks.label: Simplified Explanation
blocks.html: SRS can, by bad luck, under-represent a small subgroup. Stratification removes that risk by sampling each subgroup (urban/rural, age group, block) separately. You choose how many to take from each. With proportional allocation, each stratum’s share of the sample equals its share of the population, and the combined sample can be averaged directly. With disproportionate allocation, a small stratum is deliberately over-sampled so that it has enough cases for its own estimate. The overall estimate must then be a weighted mean (recall §2.2.2), with each stratum weighted by its population share.

blocks.label: Illustration / Example
blocks.html: A district’s under-five children are 80% rural and 20% urban. To get a usable urban estimate you sample 50 rural and 50 urban children (disproportionate allocation). Suppose 40% of rural and 20% of urban sampled children are stunted.

blocks.label: Worked Calculation
blocks.html:
1. Unweighted (wrong) district estimate: (0.40 × 50 + 0.20 × 50) ÷ 100 = 30%.
  2. Weighted estimate, using population shares: 0.80 × 40% + 0.20 × 20% = 32% + 4% = 36%.
  3. The unweighted figure understates district stunting by 6 percentage points, because it gives urban children 50% of the weight when they are only 20% of the population.

points.html: Stratification improves precision when strata are internally similar (homogeneous) and different from each other. Stratifying on an irrelevant characteristic gives little benefit.

With proportional allocation, stratified sampling gives an overall estimate that is (apart from negligible finite-population terms) never less precise than SRS of the same total size, and usually more precise. Disproportionate allocation can lower the precision of the overall estimate (the unequal weights add variance) while raising the precision of the small stratum’s own estimate.
Whenever sampling fractions differ between strata, combine them with population weights, as in step 2.

blocks.html: Cluster Sampling

blocks.label: Definition
blocks.html: Cluster sampling divides the population into naturally occurring groups (clusters) such as villages, schools or anganwadi centres, selects some clusters at random, and measures units within the selected clusters. In one-stage cluster sampling every unit in a selected cluster is measured. When units are sub-sampled within each selected cluster, the design becomes two-stage (§6.2.5).

blocks.label: Simplified Explanation
blocks.html:
SRS of households across a district sends field teams to every corner. Cluster sampling sends them to a few villages instead. It also needs a frame only of clusters (a list of villages) plus a list of households inside the few selected villages, not a household list for the whole district.

The price is precision. Households in one village share a water source, a sub-centre, an ASHA and local prices. They resemble each other more than households chosen at random from the whole district. So 25 households from one village carry less independent information than 25 households scattered across the district. This is the opposite of stratification: stratification gains precision by making sure every different group is represented; clustering loses precision because each selected group is internally alike. The size of this loss is measured by the design effect (DEFF: the variance of an estimate under the cluster design divided by its variance under SRS of the same size), defined and computed in §6.2.6.

blocks.label: Illustration / Example
blocks.html: A district has 200 villages. Instead of drawing households from all 200, you randomly select 10 villages and survey every household in them. The field team travels to 10 places, not 200. If all 200 villages had the same number of households, say 100, each household’s chance of inclusion would be 10/200 = 0.05, equal for all. Yet this is not SRS: every possible sample consists of whole villages, so a sample of 1,000 households spread thinly over 150 villages, which SRS could produce, can never occur.

points.html: Cluster sampling buys feasibility and cost at the price of precision. For the same total number of units, it is usually less precise than SRS, because units within a cluster tend to be alike.
It fits when a list of individuals does not exist but a list of clusters does.

Unequal cluster sizes create a problem: if villages are chosen with equal probability and a fixed number of households is taken from each, a household in a small village has a much higher chance of selection than one in a large village. Selecting villages with probability proportional to size (PPS, §6.2.6) fixes this.
The CBHI household survey used throughout this book took 25 households in each of 20 villages (500 households). The villages are its clusters, and §6.2.6 computes what that clustering costs.

blocks.html: Multistage Sampling

blocks.label: Definition
blocks.html: Multistage sampling selects units in two or more nested stages: first large units (primary sampling units, PSUs, such as villages), then smaller units within the selected ones (households), and possibly smaller units again (one person per household). Each stage uses its own random method.

blocks.label: Simplified Explanation
blocks.html: One-stage cluster sampling surveys every household in each selected village, which is heavy when villages are large. Multistage sampling adds a random step inside each cluster: take 22 households from each selected village instead of all of them. It keeps the travel savings of clustering while spreading the sample across more clusters, which recovers precision.

blocks.label: Illustration / Example
blocks.html:
NFHS-5 (2019–21) is the standard Indian example (IIPS, 2021; World Bank Microdata Library, 2022):

  1. Stratification. Each district is split into rural and urban strata, and rural strata are sub-stratified by village size and the SC/ST share of the population.
  2. Stage 1 (PSUs). In rural areas, villages are selected with probability proportional to size after sorting by women’s literacy (implicit stratification, §6.2.2). In urban areas, Census Enumeration Blocks are selected.
  3. Household listing. Every selected PSU is mapped and its households listed afresh, creating the second-stage frame.
  4. Stage 2 (households). “A fixed number of 22 households per cluster was selected with an equal probability systematic selection from a newly created list of households.”

In all, 30,456 PSUs were selected across 707 districts, and 636,699 households were interviewed. The design combines the methods of §6.2.2–6.2.4 with PPS (selection in proportion to size, §6.2.6): stratification, PPS cluster selection, fresh listing, and systematic selection within clusters.

points.html: Multistage designs are the norm for large household surveys because no national list of households exists, while lists of villages and enumeration blocks do (from the Census).
Precision is driven mainly by the number of PSUs, not only by the number of households; adding households within the same villages helps less and less (§6.2.6).

Do not confuse multistage with multiphase sampling. Multistage samples different units at each stage (villages, then households). Multiphase samples the same units in successive phases: a large first-phase sample gets a cheap measurement (a screening question), and a sub-sample of it gets an expensive one (a blood test).

questions.prompt: A researcher must survey households across a state but has only a list of villages, not of households. Which design fits, and why would simple random sampling of households fail here?
questions.answer: A cluster design, in practice multistage (§6.2.4–6.2.5): select villages at random (by PPS if their sizes differ), list the households in the selected villages only, then sample households within them. SRS of households needs a complete frame of every household in the state, which does not exist; building one would cost more than the survey. SRS would also scatter the field teams across the whole state.

questions.prompt: A district is 70% rural and 30% urban. A survey samples 100 rural and 100 urban households and finds that 25% of rural and 10% of urban households use a PHC for deliveries. Give the unweighted and the correctly weighted district estimate.
questions.answer: Unweighted: (0.25 × 100 + 0.10 × 100) ÷ 200 = 35 ÷ 200 = 17.5%. Weighted by population shares: 0.70 × 25% + 0.30 × 10% = 17.5% + 3.0% = 20.5%. The unweighted figure is 3 points too low, because it gives urban households half the weight when they are 30% of the population. Allocation was disproportionate, so weights are required.

questions.prompt: Stratified and cluster sampling both begin by dividing the population into groups. State the structural difference, and its effect on precision.
questions.answer: Stratified sampling samples within every group; cluster sampling samples some groups and leaves the rest out entirely. Strata are chosen to be internally alike and different from each other, so stratification removes between-stratum variation from the error and usually increases precision. Clusters are internally alike too, but because only some are sampled, that likeness means each extra unit in a cluster adds little new information, so clustering usually reduces precision (DEFF > 1). Stratification serves precision; clustering serves feasibility.

blocks.html: Survey Designs in Indian Programmes — PPS, 30×7 Cluster, LQAS, Rapid Survey and Kish Grid; Design Effect

blocks.label: Definition
blocks.html:
• Probability proportional to size (PPS) selects clusters so that each cluster’s chance of selection is proportional to its size (its population or number of households), usually by systematic selection from a cumulative list of sizes.
  • The design effect (DEFF) is the variance of an estimate under the actual design divided by its variance under SRS of the same total size: DEFF = Var(design) ÷ Var(SRS) (Bilukha, 2008). Here the variance of an estimate means its spread over repeated samples drawn by the same design (§6.5 develops this). Its square root, DEFT, is the factor by which the design inflates the standard error (the square root of that variance, §6.4 and §6.7).
  • The WHO EPI 30×7 cluster survey is a two-stage survey of 210 children, 7 in each of 30 clusters chosen by PPS, designed to estimate immunisation coverage.
  • Lot quality assurance sampling (LQAS) takes a small random sample (commonly 19) from each supervision area and classifies the area as reaching or not reaching a coverage target, using a pre-set decision rule.
  • A rapid survey is a small, quick probability survey (such as the 30×7 design or LQAS) built for programme decisions within days or weeks rather than precise estimation.
  • The Kish grid is a pre-printed selection table that picks one eligible person in a selected household at random, using only the number of eligible members and a table assigned to that household.

blocks.label: Simplified Explanation
blocks.html: These designs answer practical field questions. Villages differ in size, so how do you give every person an equal chance when you choose villages first? Use PPS. How much precision do you lose by clustering? Measure it with the DEFF. How do you get a coverage estimate in a fortnight with limited staff? Use the 30×7 design. Your block manager does not need a coverage estimate, only to know which sub-centre areas are failing: use LQAS. You have reached the household; whom do you interview? Use the Kish grid rather than whoever opens the door.

blocks.label: Derivation
blocks.html:
Why PPS gives every person the same chance. Let village i have Mᵢ persons, total M, and select k villages by PPS, then a fixed number m of persons in each selected village.

P(person selected) = P(village i selected) × P(person selected | village i selected) = (k × Mᵢ/M) × (m/Mᵢ) = k × m / M

Mᵢ cancels, so every person in the district has the same chance k × m / M, whatever the size of their village. Such a design is called self-weighting: the sample can be averaged without weights.

What the DEFF depends on. For a cluster sample with m units per cluster, the DEFF is approximately

DEFF = 1 + (m − 1) × ρ

where ρ is the intracluster correlation coefficient (ICC: the share of the outcome’s total variance that lies between clusters rather than within them; developed fully in §15.2.1). The two extremes show why the formula has this shape (a full proof is given with the ICC in §15.2.1):

  • ρ = 0: units in a cluster are no more alike than random units, so DEFF = 1 and clustering costs nothing.
  • ρ = 1: every unit in a cluster is identical, so the m units carry the information of one. DEFF = 1 + (m − 1) = m, and n units give the information of only n ÷ m clusters.

Dividing the sample size by the DEFF gives the effective sample size, n ÷ DEFF: the size of an SRS with the same precision.

blocks.label: Illustration / Example
blocks.html:
1. PPS on a cumulative list. A block has 10 villages (data/pps_villages.csv) and you must select 3 by PPS.

Village Population Cumulative Numbers assigned Selected?
PV01 1,450 1,450 1–1,450
PV02 820 2,270 1,451–2,270 Yes (1,873)
PV03 2,310 4,580 2,271–4,580
PV04 640 5,220 4,581–5,220
PV05 1,780 7,000 5,221–7,000
PV06 3,050 10,050 7,001–10,050 Yes (7,206.3)
PV07 990 11,040 10,051–11,040
PV08 1,210 12,250 11,041–12,250
PV09 2,600 14,850 12,251–14,850 Yes (12,539.7)
PV10 1,150 16,000 14,851–16,000

blocks.label: Worked Calculation (PPS)
blocks.html:
1. Total population M = 16,000. Sampling interval = 16,000 ÷ 3 = 5,333.3.
  2. Random start between 1 and 5,333: suppose the random number drawn is 1,873.
  3. Selection numbers: 1,873; 1,873 + 5,333.3 = 7,206.3; 1,873 + 2 × 5,333.3 = 12,539.7.
  4. Find each number’s range in the cumulative column: 1,873 falls in 1,451–2,270 (PV02); 7,206.3 in 7,001–10,050 (PV06); 12,539.7 in 12,251–14,850 (PV09).
  5. Selection chances differ by size: PV06 had 3 × 3,050 ÷ 16,000 = 0.572; PV04 had 3 × 640 ÷ 16,000 = 0.120.
  6. Now take m = 20 persons in each selected village. Every person’s chance is 3 × 20 ÷ 16,000 = 0.00375, the same in every village (the Derivation above).
  7. Compare choosing 3 villages by SRS (chance 3/10 each) and then 20 persons: a person in PV04 would have chance 0.3 × 20/640 = 0.0094, and a person in PV06 0.3 × 20/3,050 = 0.0020. Small-village residents would be 4.8 times over-represented, and the sample would need weights.

blocks.alt: PPS selection of three villages from a cumulative population list
blocks.caption: Figure 6.2. PPS selection of 3 of 10 villages (data/pps_villages.csv). Each village occupies a stretch of the cumulative line equal to its population, so large villages are more likely to contain a selection number. Orange: selected villages.

blocks.label: Worked Calculation (design effect in the CBHI survey)
blocks.html:
The CBHI survey has 500 households in 20 villages, m = 25 per village, and the village ICC for membership is ρ = 0.06.

  1. DEFF = 1 + (25 − 1) × 0.06 = 1 + 1.44 = 2.44.
  2. Effective sample size = 500 ÷ 2.44 ≈ 205 households. The 500 clustered households estimate membership about as precisely as 205 households chosen by SRS.
  3. DEFT = √2.44 = 1.56: standard errors are about 1.56 times their SRS values. The SRS standard error of the 30% membership prevalence is 0.021; allowing for villages it is 0.032 (the survey analysis in §15.2.2 gives an observed DEFF of 2.41, close to the formula’s 2.44).
  4. If ρ had been 1, DEFF would be 25 and the 500 households would be worth only 500 ÷ 25 = 20 households, one per village.

2. The WHO EPI 30×7 survey. The Expanded Programme on Immunization has promoted a 30-cluster design with 7 children per cluster since 1978 (Bilukha, 2008; Litvinov et al., 1986). Clusters are selected by PPS; within each, 7 eligible children (for example, aged 12–23 months) are enrolled. Surveys adapted from the WHO 30-cluster method state its working parameters as 95% confidence, a precision of ±10 percentage points and an assumed DEFF of 2 (Mugali et al., 2017). Why 210 children deliver about ±10 points is checked in §6.7, once the standard error is available. Two known weaknesses:

  • The traditional EPI method of picking households inside a cluster is not a random selection, and field teams short of time may drift towards conveniently or centrally located houses, biasing the estimate (Bilukha, 2008).
  • A design that assumes DEFF = 2 is too small when the outcome is strongly clustered. In emergency surveys, design effects of 5 and higher have been observed for vaccination coverage, and field manuals now advise calculating the sample size for each survey (Bilukha, 2008; sample-size formulas: §7.3).

3. LQAS. A district divides its area into supervision areas (sub-centre areas, for example) and interviews 19 randomly selected children aged 12–23 months in each. The programme sets an upper threshold (the target, say 80% full immunisation) and a lower threshold 30 points below it (50%), as in the Gavi LQAS toolkit, which notes that the sample size most commonly used is n = 19 (Gavi Zero-Dose Learning Hub, n.d.). A decision rule d is chosen from the binomial distribution (recall §5.7.1.2): the area “passes” if at least d of the 19 are immunised.

blocks.label: Worked Calculation (LQAS decision rule, n = 19, thresholds 80% and 50%)
blocks.html:
1. α (risk of failing an area whose true coverage is 80%: a false alarm, the Type I error of §8.3) = P(X ≤ d − 1) for X ~ Binomial(19, 0.8).
  2. β (risk of passing an area whose true coverage is only 50%: a missed problem, the Type II error of §8.3) = P(X ≥ d) for X ~ Binomial(19, 0.5).
  3. For d = 12: α = 0.023, β = 0.180. For d = 13: α = 0.068, β = 0.084. For d = 14: α = 0.163, β = 0.032.
  4. d = 13 is the only rule that keeps both errors below 10%. Rule: pass the area if 13 or more of 19 children are fully immunised; otherwise flag it for action.

LQAS classifies; it does not estimate each area’s coverage precisely. Across areas, the samples can be combined (weighted by population) into a district estimate. A global review found 805 LQAS surveys between 1984 and 2004, 266 of them on immunisation coverage (Robertson & Valadez, 2006).

4. The Kish grid. In India’s National NCD Monitoring Survey, “one adult (18-69 years) per household was selected using the World Health Organization-KISH grid” (Mathur et al., 2021). The interviewer lists the eligible members in a fixed order (in Kish’s form, males by decreasing age, then females), then reads the member’s serial number off the selection table printed on that household’s cover sheet (Kish, 1949, as described by Nemeth, n.d.). Using the grid instead of “whoever answers the door” prevents a sample full of people who are usually at home. One consequence must be handled in analysis: with one person per household, a person in a household with 4 eligible adults has one-quarter the within-household chance of a person living alone, so a person’s chance of selection is inversely proportional to the number of eligible adults in the household (Nemeth, n.d.), and estimates need weights proportional to that number.

points.html: PPS + fixed take per cluster = self-weighting. This is why the 30×7 survey and NFHS take a fixed number of units in PPS-selected clusters. A cluster larger than the sampling interval can be hit twice; it is then given two “takes” (in the example no village exceeds 5,333.3).

DEFF = Var(design) ÷ Var(SRS) ≈ 1 + (m − 1)ρ. Effective n = n ÷ DEFF. DEFF grows with the cluster size m even when ρ is small: at ρ = 0.06, 25 per cluster gives 2.44 but 7 per cluster gives 1.36. For a fixed total, more clusters with fewer units each is more precise, at a higher travel cost.
Stratification with proportional allocation usually gives DEFF below 1; clustering usually above 1; unequal weights (disproportionate allocation, Kish-grid selection) push it up.
30×7: 210 children, 30 PPS clusters, ±10 points, DEFF assumed 2. Know its logic and its two weaknesses (non-random household selection within clusters; DEFF 2 often too low).

LQAS: n = 19 per supervision area, decision rule d from the binomial so that both classification errors stay below about 10%. It answers “which areas are failing?”, not “what is each area’s coverage?”.
Kish grid: random selection of one respondent per household; requires weighting by the number of eligible members.

questions.prompt: In the PPS example, what was the chance of selection for village PV01 (population 1,450), and what is the overall chance that a given resident of PV01 is interviewed if 20 persons are taken in each selected village?
questions.answer: P(PV01 selected) = k × Mᵢ ÷ M = 3 × 1,450 ÷ 16,000 = 0.272. P(resident interviewed | PV01 selected) = 20 ÷ 1,450 = 0.0138. Overall = 0.272 × 0.0138 = 3 × 20 ÷ 16,000 = 0.00375, the same as for a resident of any other village (the design is self-weighting).

questions.prompt: A cluster survey takes 10 households in each of 30 villages (300 households). The ICC for the outcome is 0.05. Compute the DEFF and the effective sample size.
questions.answer: DEFF = 1 + (m − 1)ρ = 1 + 9 × 0.05 = 1.45. Effective sample size = 300 ÷ 1.45 = 206.9, about 207 households. The 300 clustered households are worth about 207 households drawn by SRS.

questions.prompt: Explain why an LQAS area with 12 of 19 children immunised is “flagged” under the rule in this section, and what error the programme risks by using d = 12 instead of d = 13.
questions.answer: The rule is: pass if 13 or more of 19 are fully immunised. 12 < 13, so the area is flagged as possibly below target. With d = 12, an area whose true coverage is only 50% would still pass with probability β = P(X ≥ 12 | n = 19, p = 0.5) = 0.180, about 1 in 5. Under d = 13 this risk is 0.084. The gain from d = 12 is a smaller α (0.023 instead of 0.068: fewer good areas wrongly flagged), but the programme would miss more failing areas.
